result:
I want to write about thresholds.

Not grand ones, like gates or borders, but the small invisible thresholds that divide one version of a person from another. The moment right before speaking a difficult truth. The second between hearing a familiar song and remembering who you were when you first loved it. The pause after someone says, “We need to talk,” when the old world is still technically intact.

Thresholds are strange because they are not quite arrivals and not quite departures. They belong to neither side. And yet they often matter more than the destination. We spend so much time trying to get somewhere—into confidence, into understanding, into healing, into another phase of life—that we forget the delicate, trembling space of becoming.

Maybe that’s why people are drawn to doorways, bridges, hallways, shorelines. They are physical metaphors for inner transitions. A shoreline is honest: it admits that land and water are always negotiating. A bridge says, you cannot cross without being suspended over something uncertain. A doorway frames the fact that entrance is also departure.

There are thresholds in thought, too. The line between not knowing and knowing. Sometimes it comes gently, like dawn. Other times it arrives as a crack. You realize you no longer believe what you used to. You realize you miss someone without wanting them back. You realize your anger is actually grief wearing armor. You realize you have been waiting for permission from someone who will never give it.

And once you cross that line, you can’t fully return.

That can be frightening. But it can also be beautiful. Every meaningful growth is a series of thresholds. Learning a language. Falling out of easy certainty. Becoming kinder without becoming softer in the places that need truth. Choosing rest instead of performance. Letting yourself want something without apologizing for it.

Even writing has thresholds. The blank page is one. The first sentence is another. Somewhere between the idea and the words, a small act of courage happens. Not heroic courage, necessarily. Just the ordinary kind: the willingness to begin before you are ready.

I think that may be the secret: readiness is mostly a myth. We imagine that someday we will step across calmly, fully prepared, certain of what waits on the other side. But most thresholds are crossed with a slightly racing heart, an unfinished thought, a hope disguised as curiosity.

And still we cross.
